name: Reno

stops.name: The Reno Arch
stops.teaser: A giant sign over the main street.
stops.clue: Look for a giant sign that stretches over the main street downtown. Visitors have walked under it for generations. If you get stuck, any local can point the way.
stops.safety: Cross only at crosswalks and stay on the sidewalk. This stop is outdoors in public space. Do not step into the street for a photo.
stops.field: Field notes pending: sidewalk surfaces and curb cuts have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Find the historical marker on the arch's support column. What year is it dated?
q.hint: The marker is at eye level on the east side of the east column.
q.verify: Listed on HMDB (marker dated Aug 8, 1987). Confirm on site.

then.label: The second arch
then.line: This 1963 arch stood until the current one replaced it in 1987. Photo taken in June 1973.

link.t: See the 1926 arch in UNLV Special Collections

now.label: Today's arch
now.line: The arch over Virginia Street went up in 1987 and has been relit and repainted since. Photo taken in 2021.

story: On October 23, 1926, Reno raised a steel arch over Virginia Street. It marked the completion of the Lincoln and Victory Highways and helped promote a 1927 highways exposition.

When the exposition ended, residents had grown fond of the arch, so the city kept it and ran a slogan contest. An entrant from Sacramento named Burns won $100 for "Reno, The Biggest Little City in the World."
A larger arch with plastic panels and a rotating star replaced the first one in 1963. The arch you are standing under today was installed in 1987.
stops.fact: The 1963 arch was donated to Willits, California. The town changed its slogan to welcome visitors to the redwoods.
stops.disputed: Sources disagree on when the famous slogan first appeared on the arch. One says June 1929. Another describes it as part of the arch from 1926.

claims.t: The first Reno Arch was built in 1926.
The arch switched to LED lights in 2018.
claims.why: One source says 2009 and another says 2018. Until a city record settles it, treat it as disputed.

sources.t: UNLV Northern Nevada Neon: 2018 arch photo record

spot.q: The 1973 photo shows an arch that no longer stands. About how long did that 1963 arch last before today's arch replaced it?
spot.why: It went up in 1963 and was replaced in 1987, so it stood for 24 years.

stops.name: Reno Train Depot
stops.teaser: The reason Reno exists: the railroad reached here in 1868.
stops.map: Amtrak Station, 280 N Center St, Reno, NV
stops.clue: Walk to the downtown Reno train station, the tan Spanish-style building beside the tracks, a few blocks from the arch.
stops.safety: Stay on public sidewalks and away from the tracks. Trains pass here, so keep behind the fences and cross streets only at crosswalks.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Look at the building's style and the tracks. In what year did Southern Pacific build the current depot?
q.hint: The same decade as Reno's first arch.
q.verify: Wikipedia and a historical marker say the current depot was built in 1926. Confirm on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: Passengers then
then.line: Travelers beside the station on September 7, 1931.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The depot today
now.line: The Southern Pacific depot, now used by Amtrak.

story: Reno began as a railroad town. When the first transcontinental railroad reached the Truckee Meadows in 1868, a depot stood at this site. Myron Lake, who owned a toll bridge nearby, gave the Central Pacific Railroad land for it, and lots in the new town were auctioned on May 9.

A bigger Depot Hotel replaced the first wooden depot, burned in the Great Fire of 1879, was rebuilt, and burned again in May 1889. After that the railroad built a one-story brick station with a slate roof, and a new depot opened that December.

The current stucco depot was built by the Southern Pacific in 1926 in a Mission and Spanish Revival style. In the ReTRAC project the tracks were lowered below ground through downtown. The trench opened to trains in November 2005, and the work was finished in spring 2006. The depot was added to the National Register of Historic Places on November 12, 2012, and Amtrak's California Zephyr stops here.
stops.fact: Reno's street railway ran to the depot from 1908 to 1925.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia lists the station as opened in 1868, but the building you see dates from 1926. Amtrak's move into it is dated January 2006 on a marker, and 2007 for the renovation in Wikipedia.

claims.t: A depot has stood on this spot since 1868.
claims.why: Wikipedia and a historical marker: the first depot arrived with the railroad in 1868.

claims.t: The train tracks still run at street level through downtown Reno.
claims.why: They were lowered below ground in the ReTRAC project. The trench opened in November 2005.

sources.t: Federal Highway Administration: Reno ReTRAC financing

spot.q: Slide back to 1931. One big change since then came with the ReTRAC project, which opened its trench in 2005. What was it?
options: The tracks were lowered below ground through downtown
The depot was moved across the river
The depot was torn down and rebuilt
A wooden Depot Hotel was added
spot.why: ReTRAC lowered the tracks below ground through downtown. The stucco depot itself dates from 1926.

stops.name: Virginia Street Bridge
stops.teaser: A crossing older than the city.
stops.clue: Walk south from the first arch until the street crosses the water. This crossing is older than the city itself, and a famous legend is tied to it.
stops.safety: Use the sidewalk and stay behind the railing. Do not lean over, climb, or throw anything into the river.
stops.field: Field notes pending: sidewalk width and ramps have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Look for the giant word sculpture in City Plaza, next to the bridge. What word does it spell?
q.hint: Its letters are about 12 feet tall.
q.verify: This Is Reno (May 2016) says the BELIEVE sculpture was moved to City Plaza, northeast of the bridge. Sculptures can move, so confirm on site.

then.label: The 1905 bridge
then.line: About five years after it opened, with the old Riverside Hotel rising behind it. Photo from around 1910.

ph.by: Mella Harmon, via the Online Nevada Encyclopedia

now.head: Before 2015
now.label: The 1905 bridge, last look
now.line: The concrete bridge as documented for the Historic American Engineering Record before it was replaced. The new bridge opened April 12, 2016, with four restored light fixtures from the 1905 one. It has no free photo yet.

story: In 1860, Charles Fuller built the first bridge here. Myron Lake took over in 1861 and charged tolls. In 1868 the railroad founded the town of Reno beside this crossing.

An iron bridge arrived in 1877. In 1905 a concrete bridge designed by John B. Leonard replaced it. It was one of the first reinforced concrete bridges in Nevada and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.

In 2015 the 1905 bridge was torn down as part of a flood control plan. The new bridge opened in April 2016. A 12-foot word sculpture reading BELIEVE, by Laura Kimpton and Jeff Schomberg, was moved to City Plaza beside the new bridge in May 2016.

Reno was once called the Divorce Capital of the World. A popular legend says newly divorced people tossed their wedding rings into the river from this bridge. Books and movies helped spread the story, including a 1929 novel and the 1961 film The Misfits.
stops.fact: The 2016 bridge cost about $18.3 million and is 166 feet long.
stops.disputed: The ring-tossing story is a legend. The sources we found do not say how often it happened, if at all.

claims.t: The 1905 bridge was torn down in 2015.
claims.why: Reno Historical and the Northern Nevada Business Weekly both report it.

claims.t: Newly divorced people regularly threw wedding rings off this bridge.
claims.why: It is a well-known legend, but the sources we found do not confirm it.

spot.q: The 1910 photo shows the 1905 concrete bridge. What happened to it in 2015?
options: It was torn down as part of a flood control plan
It was moved to a museum
It was turned into a footbridge
spot.why: The 1905 bridge was torn down. The new one opened in April 2016 with four restored light fixtures from the old one.

stops.name: Wingfield Park
stops.teaser: An island that has been a resort and a runway.
stops.map: Wingfield Park, 2 N Arlington Ave, Reno NV
stops.clue: Find the island in the middle of the river. It has been a resort, a runway, and a park. Look for the outdoor stage.
stops.safety: Stay away from the water's edge. River levels and currents can change quickly, so keep close together.
stops.field: Field notes pending: paths and surfaces have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Read the marker on West 1st Street. What was this island before it became a city park?
q.hint: The island's old name was Belle Isle.
q.verify: Listed on HMDB (city acquired Belle Isle in 1920). Confirm on site.

then.label: The river dam by the park
then.line: A hand-tinted photo of the Truckee River dam at Wingfield Park, around 1935.

link.t: See real archive photos at Reno Historical

now.label: The river today
now.line: The Truckee River beside downtown Reno, near Wingfield Park. Photo taken in 2015.

story: Before it was a park, this island was a resort called Belle Isle. By 1911 it had a dance hall, an open-air theater with 700 seats, and boats to rent. Visitors crossed on a footbridge.
In July 1911, aviation pioneer Eugene Ely used part of the island as a runway. A roller skating rink opened in 1912.
George Wingfield bought the island in 1920 and gave it to the city. In the late 1930s, Works Progress Administration crews built retaining walls to hold the river banks in place.
stops.fact: The amphitheater is named for Glenn Little, a longtime performer and director of the Reno Municipal Band.

claims.t: Aviation pioneer Eugene Ely used part of this park as a runway in 1911.
claims.why: Reno Historical lists it in the park's history.

claims.t: The park has always been called Wingfield Park.
claims.why: It was Belle Isle first and was renamed after Wingfield gave it to the city in 1920.

spot.q: The 1935 photo shows a dam on the Truckee River. Before it was a park, what was this island?
spot.why: By 1911 Belle Isle had a dance hall, an open-air theater with 700 seats and boats to rent.
